To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

Drosophila kikkawai, Drosophila bi- pectinata, Sphaerogastra javana and Drosophila jambulina were recorded from Townsville for the first time; Drosophila melanogaster was not recorded; D. kikkawaii and D. melanogaster were the most common species in the forest; the urban and rainforest faunas were similar in species composition, although some species were rarer in the forest;

four drosophilid species new to Australia were collected in Townsville, Queensland; that the species composition of the Townsville urban dromsophilid fauna differs considerably from that of southern Australian towns; that some species common in Townsville are rare in the natural north Queensland rain forests; that some of the commoner forest species are rare or absent in Townsville; and that the species composition and abundance of the Townsville fauna is similar to that of north Queensland rain forests.

four species new to Australia were collected in the Townsville urban area and the species composition of the Townsville drosophilid community differs substantially from that reported for southern Australia.

the ecology of Drosophilidae in the Australian rainforest, and the evolutionary relationships of the Australian fauna to the drosophilids of the Oriental region.
the ecology of the Drosophila species complex.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the drosophilid species of Townsville, although not identical, are very similar to those of northern Queensland, but differ considerably from those of southern Australia.
the Townsville urban fauna is a mixture of the forest and southern urban faunas.

the drosophilid species of Townsville are not representative of the drosophilids of the north Queensland forest, and that the drosophila of southern Australia and of north Queensland are quite distinct in their species composition.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Townsville drosophilid community has a relatively high species diversity and that it is dominated by species of the genera Drosophila and Sphaerogaster.

the Townsville drosophilid species are not only of interest in themselves as a part of the fauna of an urban area in the tropics but that their study may also contribute to our understanding of the ecology of the species in the natural forests and to the study of the origin and evolution of the fauna of Australia and of the Pacific islands.
the drosophilid species of Townsville are predominantly tropical, but with a few temperate species and some cosmopolitan forms.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Townsville drosophilid community is a subset of the drosophilid assemblage found in the surrounding natural habitats.
the urban environment in Townsville is an important habitat for drosophilids, and that it is a suitable location for future studies of the drosophilid species present in northern Queensland.
drosophilids are an excellent model system for urban entomology studies.
